summary: Defines version 1.0 of a remote variant selection algorithm, which lets a server speed up transparent content negotiation in HTTP. It was published as an experimental protocol and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: When a website has many versions of a page, this is a shortcut recipe that helps pick the right version faster. It never caught on and is now just history.

subtitle: A formula for picking the best version of a web page on the server side.

tldr.problem: Web servers can host multiple versions of the same content (languages, formats, file types), but choosing which one to send requires understanding the client's preferences. The traditional approach required extra round-trip requests.
tldr.mechanism: RVSA/1.0 defines an algorithm that multiplies quality factors from the Accept headers (media type, charset, language, features) to compute an overall quality score for each variant. The server returns the best variant if the quality is definite and high enough, otherwise it returns a list for the client to choose from.
tldr.outcome: The algorithm was designed to speed up content negotiation but never gained wide adoption. The practice of transparent content negotiation itself faded as the web moved toward simpler approaches.

facts.label: Quality formula
facts.value: Q = round5( qs * qt * qc * ql * qf )

today: RFC 2296 is Historic. Transparent content negotiation via Accept headers is rarely used in practice. Modern web applications use simpler methods such as URL-based variant selection or server-side heuristics.

sections.title: The Problem of Multiple Content Versions
sections.content:
HTTP allows a single URL to serve multiple variants of the same information—different languages, different formats (HTML, PDF, plain text), different character encodings, and other properties. A transparent content negotiation mechanism automatically picks the best variant for the client.

Traditionally, the server returns a list of available variants, and the client picks one and requests it again. This costs an extra round-trip. RFC 2296 defines a remote variant selection algorithm that lets the server choose on the client's behalf based on the Accept headers in the initial request, eliminating the second request.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of the server saying "I have 5 versions, you pick," the server can use this algorithm to say "Based on what you like, version 3 is best" and send it right away.

sections.title: How the Algorithm Works
sections.content:
The algorithm computes an overall quality score for each variant using the formula:

Q = round5( qs × qt × qc × ql × qf )

where round5 rounds to 5 decimal places, and the factors are:

  • qs: the server's inherent quality rating for the variant (e.g., "this French version is slightly better than the English one")
  • qt: the quality the client assigned to the media type (from the Accept header)
  • qc: the quality for the charset (from Accept-Charset)
  • ql: the highest quality for any language the variant offers (from Accept-Language)
  • qf: the quality for the variant's feature requirements (from Accept-Features)

The server returns the variant with the highest score, but only if two conditions are met: first, the quality must be definite (computed without wildcards in the Accept headers), and second, the variant must be a neighbor of the main resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine each version gets a score based on how much the client likes its language, format, and other properties. The server picks the one with the highest score and sends it.

sections.title: Definite vs. Speculative Quality
sections.content:
A critical distinction in RVSA/1.0 is between definite and speculative quality values. A quality is definite if it was computed without using wildcards (like `*/*` or `*`) in any Accept header. It is speculative if the algorithm had to guess or use a wildcard.

For example, if a client sends Accept: image/gif;q=0.9, */*;q=1.0, the quality for image/gif is definite (explicitly stated), but the quality for image/png is speculative (matched by the wildcard `*/*`). The algorithm will only return a choice response (pick a variant for you) if the best variant's quality is definite. Otherwise it returns a list, letting the client choose.

This conservative approach reflects the rationale that a wildcard in the Accept header means "I'm not sure about other types, so if you're guessing, ask me first."
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm is picky: it only picks a version for you if it is sure you like that version. If it had to guess (because your browser said "I like anything"), it asks you to pick instead.

sections.title: Using RVSA/1.0 in Practice
sections.content:
Clients (browsers) can optimize by sending short Accept headers by default, trusting that the remote algorithm will ask for more information if needed. A browser might send Accept: image/gif;q=0.9, */*;q=1.0 and rely on the server to ask for details before returning, say, an inferior image/tiff.

If the remote algorithm makes a different choice than the client's local algorithm would, the client has two bad options: fetch the correct variant in a second request (slow), or display the wrong version (looks random). To avoid this, the algorithm specifies that the server should not return a choice for ambiguous cases, and the client should use a local algorithm that matches the remote one.

The algorithm is also designed so that collapsing Accept-header elements (e.g., replacing `text/html;q=1.0, text/plain;q=0.8` with `text/*;q=1.0`) and omitting headers that collapse to wildcards are safe—they don't change the algorithm's result in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Browsers can send short preference lists like "I like GIFs best, but send me anything if that is all you have." The server understands this means "pick GIF if you are sure I will like it, but if you have to guess between other types, ask me first."

sections.title: Status and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 2296 defined an experimental protocol, and transparent content negotiation never gained significant adoption. The algorithm's conservatism (requiring definite quality values) made it harder to use in practice. Modern web practices favor simpler approaches: servers often use URL paths to distinguish variants (e.g., `/document.en.html` vs. `/document.fr.html`), or they use simpler heuristics based on user preferences stored on the server.

The RFC is now considered historic and is retained for reference only. No major HTTP implementation adopted this specific algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea was clever, but in practice web servers and browsers found simpler ways to handle multiple versions of content, so this algorithm was rarely used.
